target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would realistically remove school/work scheduling constraints and make voting easier for millions
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to give workers time off or paid voting time, and low-income hourly workers in retail/service jobs may still be scheduled to work and risk losing wages if they vote. So the holiday often leaves the main scheduling barrier intact for the people most in need of flexibility, and a holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday leaves work/school schedules unchanged for the people who struggle to vote
objection: A national holiday is implemented through legislation and can include legal protections requiring reasonable time to vote and preventing lost pay, so the holiday need not be only a calendar label. With those protections, Election Day being a holiday can more reliably make voting doable for low-wage workers.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday plus legislative protections would reliably eliminate the scheduling problem
objection: A holiday and actual paid time off are not the same thing: a federal holiday does not automatically force private employers to close or provide paid voting leave. Since many low-income workers can still be scheduled and still lose wages, the holiday itself does not ensure the barrier is removed.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a national holiday would reliably make voting easier for low-income workers
objection: Even if the day is labeled a federal holiday, private employers—especially in retail and service—need not close or pay workers for voting time, so the work-and-lost-wage barrier remains unless there are separate employer time-off mandates and enforcement.

target: AG2’s assumption that a holiday leaves schedules unchanged in practice
objection: Federal holidays generally do change schedules in practice: schools close and many workplaces adjust hours or staffing, so the school/work conflict that keeps people from voting would be meaningfully reduced. International practice also shows this is workable, since many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not reliably reduce the scheduling barrier because private employers may stay open
objection: A holiday can still reduce the barrier even if some employers remain open, because it creates a predictable voting window and changes the national expectation around the day. That shifts schedules, pressures employers, and aligns with international precedent for elections on weekends or holidays.

target: AG2’s claim that employer closure or paid leave is necessary for the holiday to help
objection: The holiday can also reduce the time cost of voting itself by increasing election-day staffing and lowering waiting and administrative friction at polling places, so workers may need less time away from work even if private employers stay open.

target: AG2’s claim that school closures do not meaningfully help because work remains the main constraint
objection: Closing public schools on Election Day would remove a major part of the scheduling conflict for parents and caregivers, giving them a daytime voting window and directly reducing the school-based barrier to voting.

target: AG1’s claim that school closure creates a predictable daytime voting window for parents/caregivers
objection: Many parents and caregivers still cannot vote in a daytime window because they remain constrained by paid work schedules and lost-wage risk; school closure does not change employer scheduling and can also increase daytime childcare burdens.

target: AG1’s overall case that making Election Day a national holiday is the best policy for turnout
objection: Compared with direct reforms like automatic voter registration or state laws requiring employer time off, a holiday is a blunt policy that does not reliably remove the biggest costs of voting and can disproportionately leave low-income hourly workers still facing lost wages.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is a blunt, unreliable policy that doesn’t remove the main costs of voting
objection: A federal holiday directly targets the scheduling barriers that prevent millions from voting by disrupting school and work routines, lowering the need to sacrifice wages or rigid work time. It also treats voting as a national civic celebration rather than a chore, which elevates participation and aligns with broad public and international support.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only addresses one time-related friction and does not reliably remove the biggest costs of voting
objection: The holiday changes real-world routines, especially school schedules and many institutions’ operating hours, which reduces the overlap between voting hours and required attendance. It also lowers administrative and waiting friction because election operations run as a planned public event, so it directly targets the scheduling bottleneck.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status is just a label and not an effective change
objection: The key barrier is the overlap of voting hours with school and work routines, and a national holiday changes those routines in practice by closing or disrupting schools and prompting many institutions to alter hours. That makes the holiday a direct scheduling fix rather than an ineffective symbolic gesture.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday mainly helps already-flexible voters and not those blocked by schedules
objection: A federal holiday reduces the central cause of voting costs—rigid school and work routines—by changing when people are expected to be in class or at work, thereby lowering time and scheduling burdens for millions. It is therefore not merely an uneven benefit for flexible voters.

target: AG2’s claim that Election Day as a holiday is mainly symbolic and does not alter availability
objection: Putting Election Day on the federal holiday calendar changes the day that institutions plan around: public schools close or disrupt schedules, many workplaces adjust operating hours, and the broader day becomes a planned civic event, all of which lower the real cost of voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reliably removes the main barrier because schools and workplaces adjust
objection: Even if schools close and some institutions adjust, many low-income voters still cannot vote without losing wages because private employers may not give time off and polling hours do not automatically become more flexible. School closures mainly help caregivers tied to school routines and do not solve the work-schedule problem for many hourly workers.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not meaningfully change the time-and-income cost of voting
objection: A national holiday changes more than calendars: it typically causes public school closure and holiday-hour adjustments across many workplaces, reducing the overlap between required attendance and voting time. That lowers the lost-wage tradeoff and can also reduce waiting and administrative friction, making the holiday a system-wide scheduling fix.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status is just a label and does not change real availability
objection: Placing Election Day on the federal holiday calendar changes when people are required to be in school or on normal weekday work routines, so the overlap between polls-open time and mandatory attendance is reduced. Because that is the core barrier, the holiday itself is designed to make more people available to vote.
